# Approximating the Longest Common Subsequence problem within a sub-polynomial factor in linear time Negev Shekel Nosatzki
Columbia University
`ns3049@columbia.edu` **Abstract** The Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) of two strings is a fundamental string similarity measure with a classical dynamic programming solution taking quadratic time. Despite significant efforts, little progress was made in improving the runtime. Even in the realm of approximation, not much was known for linear time algorithms beyond the trivial \(\sqrt{n}\)-approximation. Recent breakthrough result provided a \(n^{0.497}\)-factor approximation algorithm [HSSS19], which was more recently improved to a \(n^{0.4}\)-factor one[BCD21]. The latter paper also showed a \(n^{2-2.5\alpha}\) time algorithm which outputs a \(n^\alpha\) approximation to the LCS, but so far no sub-polynomial approximation is known in truly subquadratic time. In this work, we show an algorithm which runs in _O(n_) time, and outputs a \(n^{o(1)}\)-factor approxi- mation to LCS(_x,y_), with high probability, for any pair of length _n_ input strings. Our entire algorithm is merely an efficient black-box reduction to the Block-LIS problem, introduced very recently in [ANSS21], and solving the Block-LIS problem directly.

## 1 Introduction

The Longest Common Subsequence problem (LCS) is a classical string alignment problem. Formally, given two strings _x,y_ of length _n_ over alphabet \(\Sigma\), the longest common subsequence between _x_ and _y_ is the largest string which appears as a subsequence in both _x_ and _y_. The (length of the) LCS has a classical dynamic programming solution in quadratic time \[WF74\].

LCS is also a fundamental string similarity measure of key importance both in theory and practice, and therefore has been extensively studied during the course of the past 50 years \[UAH76, Hir77, HS77, AG87, EGGI92, SW07, RSSS19, RS20\], with the main goal of improving the run-time from polynomial towards close(r) to linear.

Despite significant attention, little progress was made, and the runtime has improved by logarithmic factors only \[MP80\]. More recently, fine-grained hardness results helped explaining the lack of progress, showing that any truly subquadratic solution for LCS would refute the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH)\[ABW15, BK15\]. Moreover, for the LCS problem in particular, it was later shown that even a high polylogarithmic speedup would be surprising \[AHWW16, AB18\].

Even before the above hardness results, researchers started considering faster algorithms that approximate the LCS, but there as well the progress has been slow. The trivial \(\sqrt{n}\)-factor approximation was only recently improved to ≈_n_<sup>0.497</sup> \[HSSS19\] and even more recently to _n_<sup>0.4</sup> \[BCD21\]. In parallel, a parametrized version was developed which gives a subquadratic solution with improved approximation when the longest common subsequence is promised to be above a certain threshold \[RSSS19\].

In contrast, the progress for the corresponding Edit Distance problem has been more "rosy", with a series of advances \[BJKK04, BES06, AKO10, CDG<sup>+</sup>18\], recently culminating in a near-linear time, constant factor approximation algorithm \[AN20\].

### 1.1 Main result

Our main result is a sub-polynomial factor approximation algorithm for LCS, which runs in linear time.

**Theorem 1.** LCS_<sub>n</sub> can be approximated up to n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>_-factor, with high probability, and in O(n_) _time._

While we do not track the exact approximation factor in our analysis, we note it is \(exp\left(\frac{log(n)}{log^clog(n)}\right)\) for some absolute constant _c_. Interesting enough, we could not find a way to significantly improve the bound above, obtainable in linear time, even if one can afford _n_<sup>1.99</sup> runtime. This relates to the issue of balancing of dense and sparse cases described in \[ANSS21\], which is the core component of our algorithm.

To improve the bound, one would need to find a more efficient way to solve the Block-LIS algorithm from \[ANSS21\].

One of the implications of this paper is that an affirmative resolution to the open question posed in \[ANSS21\] would yield surprising results, and in particular, a near-linear time, \((1+\epsilon)\) approximation to LCS, which also provides near-linear \(\epsilon n\) additive approximation to the edit distance.

## 2 Preliminaries

### 2.1 Definitions

**Sequences.** Fix alphabet \(\Sigma\). We denote \(x\in\Sigma^n\) as a length _n_ sequence.

For a sequence _x_, we denote by \(\psi(x):\Sigma\rightarrow\unknown\), the count vector of letters in _x_, i.e., \(\psi(x)_c\unknown|x^{-1}(c)|\) for any \(c\in\Sigma\).

We also define integer block sequence \(z\in\unknown^{n\times k}\), and denote |_z_| as the count of all integers in all the blocks (with repetitions).

**Monotone sets.** We define monotone sets as follows:

**Definition 2.** _We say that a set_ \(P\subseteq\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\) _is_ monotone _iff for all_ \(((i,k),(j,l))\in P\times P\)_, we have (i)_ \(i=j\Leftrightarrow l=k\)_; and (ii)_ \(i<j\Leftrightarrow k<l\).

One can observe that

\(\mathrm{LCS}(x,y)=\mathrm{max}_{P\subseteq[n]\times[n]P\text{is monotone}}\sum_{(i,j)\in P}\mathbf{1}[x_i=y_j]\)

**The Block-LIS problem.** The Block-LIS problem was defined in \[ANSS21\]<sup>1</sup>. In Block-LIS, the main input consists of _n_ blocks of (at most) _k_ elements each, and each block can contribute at most one of its elements to a subsequence. Formally, for an integer block sequence \(z\in\mathbb{N}^{n\times k}\), Block-LIS(_z_) is the length of a maximal sub-sequence \(\mathsf{OPT}\unknown\{(w_1,z_w)\}_{w\in[n]\times[k]}\) such that OPT is monotone.

**Other notations.** Fix vectors \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}^n\), then min(_a,b_) (respectively max(_a,b_)) is defined, as the vector of minimums (respectively, maximums) for each (_a<sub>i</sub>,b<sub>i</sub>_) pair. Also, the notation \(\oplus\) means the direct sum.

## 2.2 Main technique - Block-LIS reduction

Our construction boils down to a formulation of the LCS problem as a (larger) LIS problem, and solve the LIS problem directly. Our reduction at its core is reminiscent to ideas introduced in \[HS77, AG87\], with two important differences:

1. We provide a simplified approach by direct "black-box" reduction to a LIS problem which is then solved directly. In particular, we reduce to the Block-LIS problem. As a result, the entire construction and proof takes roughly 1.5 pages.<tbc>

2. We show that the number of "matching pairs" is always bounded by \(2n\cdot\mathrm{LCS}(x,y)\) using norm inequalities, implying the linear runtime from Lemma 4.3 in \[ANSS21\].

In particular, we restate the following Definition and Theorem:

**Definition 3.** _\[ANSS21\] For_ \(\alpha\ge 1\) _and_ \(\beta>0\)_, an_ \((\alpha,\beta)\)_-approximation_ \(\hat{q}\) _of a quantity q is an_ \(\alpha\)_- multiplicative and_ \(\beta\) _additive estimation of q, i.e.,_ \(\hat{q}\in[q/\alpha-\beta,q]\).

**Theorem 4.** _\[ANSS21\] Fix_ \(n,k\in\mathbb{N}\) _and_ \(z\in\mathbb{N}^{n\times k}\)_. For any_ \(\lambda=o(1)\)_, there exists a randomized non- adaptive algorithm_ A_<sub>BL</sub> that solves Block-LIS up to_ \((\alpha,\lambda n)\)_-approximation, where_ \(\alpha=\left(\frac{|z|}{\lambda n}\right)^{o(1)}\) _using_ \(\left(\frac{|z|}{\lambda n}\right)\cdot n^{o(1)}\) _time._

**Block-LIS tion for LCS.** To prove Theorem 1, we formulate the LCS problem as a single string Block-LIS. Given \(x,y\in\Sigma^n\), we define an integer block sequence _z_ such that each _z<sub>i</sub>_ is a block of all \(j\in[n]\) indices where _y<sub>j</sub>=x<sub>i</sub>_. Formally:

\(z\unknown\oplus_{i\in[n]}\left\{y^{-1}\left(x_i\right)\right\}.\) (1)

We claim the following equivalence:

**Claim 5.** _Block-LIS(z_)=LCS(_x,y)._

<sup>1</sup>The original definition of Block-LIS included another extension which is not relevant for our reduction, and hence was omitted for exposition.

_Proof._ First, observe that any common subsequence of _x_ and _y_ has a monotone set \(P\subseteq[n]\times[n]\) where _x<sub>i</sub>=y<sub>j</sub>_ for all \((i,j)\in P\). Now, since \(j\in y^{-1}(x_i)\), then the second coordinates of _P_ are also an increasing subsequence of _z_.

Similarly, consider the coordinates of an increasing subsequence \(W\subseteq[n]\times[k]\). Then \(\{(w_1,z_w)\}_{w\in W}\) is a monotone set where _x_<sub>_w_<sub>1</sub></sub>=_y<sub>z<sub>w</sub></sub>_, and hence _x_ and _y_ has a common subsequence of the same length.

Our entire algorithm is merely an efficient implementation of the above reduction, and solving it using Theorem 4. In particular, we show the following:

**Lemma 6.** _Suppose there exists an algorithm_ A_<sub>BL</sub> which_ \(\left(f\left(\frac{|z|}{\lambda n}\right),\lambda n\right)\) _approximates Block-LIS in time_ \(t\left(\frac{|z|}{\lambda n},n\right)\)_. Then, there exists an algorithm_ A<sub>LCS</sub> _approximating_ LCS_<sub>n</sub> up to a factor_ \((1+o(1))\cdot f(n\cdot\mathrm{log}n)\) _in_ \(t\left(O(n\cdot\mathrm{log}(n)),n\right)+O(n)\) _time._

_Proof of Theorem 1 using Theorem 4 and lemma 6._ The proof follow almost immediately from Theorem 4 and lemma 6. However, a direct invocation of the statements only yields _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> time algorithm. To obtain linear time, we first subsample \(U\subseteq[n]\) i.i.d. at rate _n_<sup>-_o_(1)</sup>, and then apply the statements on _x<sub>U</sub>_ and _y<sub>U</sub>_, noting \(\mathrm{LCS}(x_U,y_U)\in[n^{-o(1)},1]\cdot\mathrm{LCS}(x,y)\). The resulting runtime is |_U_|<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>=_O(n_) as needed.

## 2.3 Useful lower bound for the LCS using Hölder’s inequality

**Hölder’s inequality.** A classical norm inequality which says that \(\langle x,y\rangle\le\left\|x\right\|_{1/p}\cdot\left\|y\right\|_{1/q}\) for any _p+q_=1. In particular, \(\langle x,y\rangle\le\left\|x\right\|_\infty\cdot\left\|y\right\|_1\). Such inequality can be extended to show the following bound:

**Claim 7.** _Fix_ \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\)_. Then,_ \(\langle x,y\rangle\le\left\|\mathrm{min}\{x,y\}\right\|_\infty\cdot(\left\|x\right\|_1+\left\|y\right\|_1)\).

_Proof._ Let _a_=min{_x,y_} and _b_=max{_x,y_}. Then, by Hölder’s inequality,

\(\langle x,y\rangle=\langle a,b\rangle\le\left\|a\right\|_\infty\cdot\left\|b\right\|_1=\left\|\mathrm{min}\{x,y\}\right\|_\infty\cdot\left\|\mathrm{max}\{x,y\}\right\|_1\le\left\|\mathrm{min}\{x,y\}\right\|_\infty\cdot(\left\|x\right\|_1+\left\|y\right\|_1).\)

**Simple lower bound for the LCS.** We next state a useful fact about the minimal LCS of two strings:

**Fact 8.** \(\mathrm{LCS}(x,y)\ge\left\|\mathrm{min}\{\psi(x),\psi(y)\}\right\|_\infty\).

_Proof._ That fact is immediate, since if each of _x_ and _y_ contain _k_ copies of the same letter _c_, then _c<sup>k</sup>_ is a common subsequence to both _x_ and _y_.

We combine the above to show the following lower bound on the LCS:

**Lemma 9.** \(\mathrm{LCS}(x,y)\ge\frac{|z|}{2n}\) .

_Proof._ Observe that by construction \(|z|=\langle\psi(x),\psi(y)\rangle\). Now, invoking Claim 7 and fact 8, we obtain:

\(|z|\le\left\|\mathrm{min}\{\psi(x),\psi(y)\}\right\|_\infty\cdot(\left\|\psi(x)\right\|_1+\left\|\psi(y)\right\|_1)\le 2n\cdot\mathrm{LCS}(x,y),\)

which implies the Lemma.

One direct implication of the above is a simple deterministic and exact algorithm for LCS in time \(O(n\ell\mathrm{log}(\ell))\), where \(\ell=\mathrm{LCS}(x,y)\). While we do not derive it in this paper, one can observe this can be done by simply reducing the LCS problem to Block-LIS, and solving it directly as a standard LIS problem, which takes _O_(|_z_|log(LIS(_z_))) time.

## 3 Reduction Algorithm

In this section we prove Lemma 6. Namely, we are given an algorithm A<sub>BL</sub> for solving Block-LIS(_z_) with additive error parameter \(\lambda\), and we use it to estimate LCS(_x,y_).

The algorithm is the straight-forward one:

### 3.1 Analysis

We show the above algorithm provides the guarantees of Lemma 6.

_Proof of Lemma 6._ First, let us argue \(\widehat{\ell}\in\left[\frac{1-o(1)}{f(nlogn)},1\right]\cdot\text{LCS}(x,y)\).

**Upper Bound.** The upper-bound is immediate since the output of A<sub>BL</sub> is promised to be at most Block-LIS(_z_)=LCS(_x,y_), and since \(d\le\text{LCS}(x,y)\) from Lemma 9.

**Lower Bound.** Let \(\widehat{\ell_\mathcal{A}}\) be the output of A<sub>BL</sub>. Then, we are guaranteed

\(\widehat{\ell_\mathcal{A}}\ge\frac{\text{Block-LIS}(z)}{f(|z|/\lambda)}-\lambda n=\frac{\text{LCS}(x,y)}{f(nlogn)}-\frac{2d}{logn}.\)

Therefore, \(\widehat{\ell}=max\{\widehat{\ell_\mathcal{A}},d\}\ge(1-o(1))\cdot\frac{\text{LCS}(x,y)}{f(nlogn)}\) as needed.

Last, we show the runtime is at most \(t\left(O(n\cdot log(n)),n\right)+O(n)\).

**Runtime Analysis.** The runtime for the first 2 steps is clearly _O(n_). It remains to show the runtime on the Block-LIS algorithm, which is promised to be at most

\(t\left(\frac{|z|}{\lambda n},n\right)=t\left(\frac{2d}{\lambda},n\right)=t\left(O(n\cdot log(n)),n\right).\)

This concludes the proof.
